segments.original: During the first decade of the 21st century, we saw British cinema scoop up a series of awards and director Danny Boyle (b. 1956) venture into Bollywood territory: Slumdog Millionaire (2008) made headlines by winning eight Oscars, including Best Picture.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Acclaimed director Mike Leigh (b. 1943) found success with Vera Drake (2004), the story of a woman who performs illegal abortions, while newcomer Stephen Daldry (b. 1961) burst onto the scene with Billy Elliot (2000), his upbeat drama about a boy from a mining community who learns to dance. The film was acclaimed by critics worldwide and caught Hollywood's attention.

segments.original: British society and its customs were captured both through the lens of Pawel Pawlikowski (b. 1957) in My Summer of Love (2004), which tells the bittersweet story of a teenage romance, and - albeit from a very different angle - by the French co-production directed by Stephen Frears (b. 1941), The Queen (2006), about the death of Princess Diana.

segments.original: Although produced with American money, the Harry Potter franchise (2001-2011) was filmed in the United Kingdom at Leavesden Film Studios, located in Hertfordshire. Its films star local actors and count Englishmen Mike Newell (b. 1942) and David Yates (b. 1963) among their directors. The epic story of the young wizard is one of the highest-grossing film series of all time.

tracks.title: Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Of all the award winners of this new millennium, the most idiosyncratic was the claymation Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit (2005), by Nick Park (b. 1958) and Steve Box (b. 1967). Produced by Bristol-based Aardman Features and DreamWorks Animation, this inventive and hilarious film, packed with gadgets from the absent-minded inventor Wallace, slapstick humor, and comic references to the world of cinema, delights adults and children alike.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: A British film that covered more familiar territory, The Constant Gardener (2005), won numerous awards thanks to the powerful performances of its cast. It stars Ralph Fiennes as the disillusioned British diplomat Justin Quayle, who sets out to uncover the truth behind the murder of his idealistic wife (Rachel Weisz), a human rights activist, after she stumbles upon the shady practices of a major pharmaceutical company in Kenya. Although the plot is complex, Brazilian director Fernando Meirelles (b. 1955) does an excellent job with the exposition without slowing the pace of the narrative.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: While the revival of British cinema in the 1990s revolved around period dramas and romantic comedies, the 2000s brought weightier films and a United Kingdom willing to reflect on its not-so-distant colonial past in The Last King of Scotland (2006), directed by Scotsman Kevin Macdonald (b. 1967). This low-budget picture became a box office hit thanks to a screenplay co-written by Peter Morgan, co-writer of The Queen, and to a forceful performance by Forest Whitaker (b. 1961) as the Ugandan dictator General Idi Amin, which earned him an Oscar. The mesmerizing Whitaker manages to project the intimidating, murderous nature of this deranged leader in such a way that he comes across as a deeply flawed human being rather than a stereotypical figure of evil.
